doc.title: Jones Hank — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: GG Grice and the Donald Byrd jazz lab group; record dates with unknown labels
summary: Jones was never in the lab group but recorded with Grice; recording names were often invented later, and musicians rarely knew who paid.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: I was picking up on that thing with GG Grice. That GG Grice, Donald Byrd jazz band, what are your recollections on what that group was about? Was it…

I don't know that much about it, but their name suggests, at least to me, that they did a bunch of experimental playing. It probably wasn't down the middle, straight-line jazz, but little excursions. It was that kind of stuff. It was something like what they do today that is called avant-garde perhaps. I think in GG’s case, GG has always kept 1 foot on the ground. He never got completely off the ground with that off-the-wall type of music that we talked about. He was more of a middle of the roader and he was an experimenter. I think his little jaunt with that group you mentioned, that Lab Group, was just a diversion at the time. His main interest was straight ahead jazz or, it was bebop which he was into.
Did it afford you an opportunity to explore composing? Was that encouraged by members in the group?
I was never a member of that particular group. I was always writing tends. I had always written tunes. I had about six tunes back then. I think, it was at least six, all which GG covered.

We did see that you were protected because I had to copyright the whole book. It took you and he, when you were together, in case any of his tunes were in his book, he was going to see that he was protected. In order to prepare…He named it, a tune with Hank and GG Grice. I would say that he made sure that Hank would be protected in case one of his tunes was on his line or what have you.
In other words, he returned the copyright rights to me. They are now in Thank.
He had the copyright himself, and during the book he had the tunes to him and Hank. We still have that copyright.
Did you come to the relationship with him through Donald Byrd?

No. I think I met GG on a recording date that had nothing to do with Donald Byrd. To my knowledge, I don’t think I have ever recorded with Donald Byrd. I did one of the Newport Festival things with Donald Byrd. He picked me up at Hotel 5 one day and we drove from there to Newport.
You were not feeling well (Laughs). He had a wrath.
You’re on a recording with…you’re on two recordings with GG Grice and that band.
Yes, with that band. You see, I suspect that at the time of the recording, it wasn't known by that name. I kind of suspect that it was just a bunch of guys they
got together and then they named it after the record came out. I think that is probably happened.
Actually, I have one on Verve, one on RCA, and one on Jubilee and they were all made within a month of each other.

…of each other. At the time they were made, they were made with the same group but not under that name. I think that is what happened. I don’t know. I am just guessing. Many times when you go on a record date, you don't know the whys, or the how’s, for the wherefores. Sometimes, you didn't know who was going to pay you. You hope that you would get paid, and most of the time you did, but you never really knew.
So, it’s “Okay, I’m supposed to be at a certain place.”
“Play the music, wash your hands and go home!” (Laughs)
